concepts.title: Personal Area Network (PAN)
concepts.explanation:
A personal area network (PAN) is the smallest type of network. It usually connects just a few devices that all belong to one person, and their purpose is to meet that person's personal needs. The devices are normally very close together, within a few metres. Importantly, in a PAN all the network hardware belongs to the user — the cables, the wireless links, everything.

Here is an everyday example. Imani has a smartwatch that counts the steps she walks each day. She connects the smartwatch to her mobile phone so she can see the data on a bigger screen. The watch and the phone are right next to each other, they both belong to Imani, and they connect wirelessly using Bluetooth. That is a PAN.
concepts.example: A PAN can also be wired. Leo connects his laptop to a printer in the Hargeisa office using a USB cable to print an invoice. The two devices are close together, they connect just to meet Leo's need to print, and Leo owns the cable. That is also a PAN. So a PAN can be wireless or wired — what makes it a PAN is that it is small, personal, close together, and owned by the user.

concepts.title: Local Area Network (LAN)
concepts.explanation:
A local area network (LAN) is bigger than a PAN. It can connect many devices — from a handful to hundreds — but they are all located within one building or one small site, such as a school, an office or a home. The network hardware belongs to the organisation that owns the site.

Picture the Horizon Distributors office in Hargeisa. There are several computers, a shared printer, and a switch and router in the corner. All the computers are connected to the switch using Ethernet cables, so staff can share files and use the one printer. Every device is inside the same building, and the cables and switch belong to the business. That is a LAN. A school computer lab is another classic example: twenty computers and a printer, all connected, all in one room.
concepts.example: A LAN does not have to be fully wired. Many LANs also let devices join over Wi-Fi through a wireless access point. What makes it a LAN is not whether it uses cables or Wi-Fi — it is that the connected devices are all in one local place, owned by the same person or organisation.

concepts.title: Wide Area Network (WAN)
concepts.explanation:
A wide area network (WAN) connects devices spread across a large geographic area. This could be across a town, across a whole country, or even across several countries. The devices can be very far apart. A WAN often uses a mixture of wired and wireless connections.

Here is the key difference from a LAN: in a WAN, not all the hardware belongs to the user. Some belongs to other companies, especially an internet service provider (ISP). An ISP is a company that provides an internet connection to a home or business, and it owns the long-distance cables that run between towns and cities.

Now think about Horizon Distributors again. When the Mogadishu branch opens, the Hargeisa LAN and the Mogadishu LAN will need to connect. They do this through the internet: each office's router connects to an ISP, and the ISPs are joined by long-distance cables and links that stretch between the two cities. The two local networks, joined across a huge distance, form a WAN. The offices own their own routers, but the ISP owns the cables in between.

The internet itself is the largest WAN of all. It connects billions of devices worldwide. A video-streaming service is another example: films are stored on servers in one place, and people all over the country watch them on devices connected across a WAN.

Here is a picture of the WAN that links the two Horizon Distributors offices. Read it as a diagram in words — two local networks joined by ISPs across the internet:

Two LANs joined across the internet form a WAN

+---------------------+ +---------------------+

| PCs + printer | | PCs + printer |

| switch + router | | switch + router |

+----------+----------+ +----------+----------+

[ ISP ] ======= the INTERNET ======= [ ISP ]

The internet began in the 1970s as a tiny experiment called ARPANET, which connected only a few computers in a handful of American cities. It slowly grew into the worldwide network we use today, now linking billions of devices. Every one of those devices is part of the biggest WAN on Earth.
concepts.example: "The internet and a WAN are exactly the same thing." Not quite. The internet IS a WAN - in fact the biggest one - but not every WAN is the internet. A large bank could build its own private WAN linking branches in different cities without letting the public onto it. So: the internet is a WAN, but a WAN is not always the internet.

concepts.title: Network Topologies: The Shape of a Network
concepts.explanation:
Once you have several devices in a LAN, you must decide how to arrange the connections between them. The layout, or shape, of a network is called its topology. Choosing a topology is a real decision when you design a network, so Horizon Distributors will need to pick one for its office. There are four common topologies to know: bus, star, ring and mesh.

In a bus topology, every device connects to a single central cable called the backbone. Data travels along this one cable, and each end of it has a terminator to stop signals bouncing back. A bus is cheap and uses little cable, but it has a big weakness: if the backbone cable breaks, the whole network fails. And if many devices send data at once, they collide and the network slows down.

Bus topology - all devices share one backbone cable

In a star topology, every device connects to a central device, usually a switch. This is the most common layout for LANs today, and it is what Horizon Distributors will most likely use. Its great strength is reliability: if one cable breaks, only that one device goes offline — the rest keep working. It is also easy to add a new device: just plug it into the switch. The trade-offs are that it uses more cable, and if the central switch itself fails, the whole network goes down.

Star topology - every device connects to a central switch

In a ring topology, devices are connected in a loop, and data travels around the ring from one device to the next until it reaches its destination. Rings can be efficient, but if one device or connection in the loop breaks, it can stop data reaching the rest of the ring.

Ring topology - data travels around a loop

In a mesh topology, devices are connected to many other devices, so there are several possible paths for data. If one path is broken, data simply takes another route. This makes a mesh extremely reliable — there is no single point of failure. The downside is cost: a full mesh needs a huge amount of cabling. The internet is arranged rather like a giant mesh, which is one reason it keeps working even when parts of it fail.

Mesh topology - many paths between devices

concepts.title: Wired Connections: Copper vs Fibre Optic
concepts.explanation:
When a network uses a wired connection, the wire is almost always one of two kinds: a copper cable or a fibre optic cable. They carry data in completely different ways, and each has its own strengths.

Copper cables are made of thin strands of copper wire. They are the traditional cables that have been used in networks for decades. They carry data as electrical signals travelling down the metal. Copper is cheap to make and easy to install, partly because so many countries already have copper cabling in the ground from old telephone networks. Its data speed is modest — the basic cabling described here reaches around 200 Mbps. Copper has two weaknesses: it can suffer from electromagnetic interference (when nearby electrical signals disturb the signal in the cable), so it needs a thick outer case to protect it. Everyday copper cables include Ethernet cables, HDMI cables (which carry high-definition video and sound) and, most likely, your phone charger cable.

Fibre optic cables are made of many thin strands of glass. They are a more modern cable, and instead of electricity they carry data as pulses of light travelling down the glass. Fibre is extremely fast, reaching 10 Gbps or more — many times faster than copper. Because it uses light, not electricity, it is not affected by electromagnetic interference at all, and the cable can be thinner because it needs no thick protective case. The trade-offs are that fibre is more expensive to make and harder to install, since most places already have copper in place. Fibre is designed mainly for long distances, which is why countries are laying it underground between towns and cities and using more of it to carry the internet's traffic.
concepts.example: Light travelling down a fibre optic cable can carry so much data that a single hair-thin strand of glass can handle thousands of phone calls and video streams at the same time. That is why the long-distance cables that connect cities - and even the cables that run under the sea between continents - are made of fibre, not copper.

concepts.title: Wired vs Wireless: Advantages and Disadvantages
concepts.explanation:
Devices can join a network with a wired connection (a cable) or a wireless connection (such as Wi-Fi). You might wonder: if wireless is so convenient, why do wired connections still exist? The answer is that each has real advantages, and the best choice depends on the job. Here is how they compare across four important ideas.

Reliability. Wired connections are usually more reliable, because a cable does not suffer interference from walls or other radio waves. Wireless can be less reliable, as walls, distance and other signals can interrupt it.

Security. Wired connections are usually more secure. To break in, a hacker would have to physically reach the network hardware and plug in. Wireless is easier to attack, because a hacker within range might guess or steal the password and connect without ever touching the hardware.

Speed. Wired connections normally have a faster data transmission speed than wireless connections.

Ease and cost. Wireless is easier and cheaper to set up and expand: to add a device you just enter the password, and you only need a wireless access point. Wired is more expensive and fiddly: you must buy cables, find space for them, and keep the wires tidy and safe — which gets harder as you add more devices.

So for Horizon Distributors, the confidential data about customers and money is a strong reason to use wired connections for the main office computers — they are faster and harder to hack. But staff phones and a visitor's laptop might join over Wi-Fi for convenience, protected by a strong password. Good network designers mix both, choosing each for the right reason.

"Wireless is always better because there are no annoying cables." Not true. Wireless is more convenient, but a wired connection is usually faster, more reliable and more secure. For private business data - or a hospital, or a bank - the security of a cable often matters more than the convenience of Wi-Fi.

Part B — 3.2 Data Transmission and Security
concepts.example: You now know the different types of network and how they are wired. In this part you will learn what actually happens when data travels across one — how it is broken up and addressed, how mistakes creep in and are caught, and how we keep the data secret and safe from people who should not see it. This is exactly what Horizon Distributors needs to protect its customers and its money.

concepts.title: Data Packets: Travelling in Small Pieces
concepts.explanation:
When you send a photo or a message across a network, the data does not travel as one big lump. Instead, the network breaks it into many small pieces called data packets. This is one of the most important ideas about how modern networks work.

Imagine Maya wants to post a long letter to Karim, but she may only use small envelopes. She tears the letter into pages, puts each page in its own envelope, and writes on every envelope three things: the destination address, her own return address, and a page number so the pages can be put back in the right order. Data packets work in exactly the same way. Each packet carries a header (the addresses and a sequence number), a payload (a small piece of the actual data), and a trailer with error-checking information.

+-------------------------------------------+

+-------------------------------------------+

| - a small piece of the actual data |

+-------------------------------------------+

| - error-checking information |

+-------------------------------------------+
concepts.example: The packets travel across the network and may even take different routes to reach the same place. At the destination, the receiving device uses the sequence numbers to put them back together in the correct order. If a packet is lost or damaged on the way, the receiver notices a piece is missing and asks for just that packet to be sent again. This is clever for two reasons: many people can share one network at the same time, and a single damaged packet never ruins the whole message — only one small piece needs resending.

concepts.title: Protocols: The Rules of Communication
concepts.explanation:
For two devices to understand each other, they must follow the same rules. A protocol is an agreed set of rules for how data is sent and received. Think of it like good manners in a conversation: if everyone agrees to take turns and speak the same language, the conversation works. If not, it is chaos. Protocols are the shared 'language and manners' of networks.

There are many protocols, each for a different job. A few you should know:

TCP/IP — the core rules of the internet. They control how data is split into packets, how each packet is addressed, and how the packets are reassembled at the other end.

HTTP — the rules for sending web pages from a web server to your browser.

HTTPS — the secure version of HTTP. The 's' means the data is encrypted as it travels, so it stays private. When Maya checks a supplier's website, she should look for https and a padlock before typing anything private.
concepts.example: You do not need to memorise every protocol. The big idea is simple: a protocol is a shared set of rules that lets very different devices, made by different companies in different countries, all talk to each other reliably.

concepts.title: When Data Goes Wrong: Errors in Transmission
concepts.explanation:
Computers send data as binary — long streams of bits, where each bit is a 0 or a 1. A group of 8 bits is called a byte, and one byte often stands for a single character. While data is travelling, a bit can sometimes get corrupted: it flips from a 1 to a 0, or from a 0 to a 1. Even one flipped bit can turn a character into a completely different one, so errors matter.

Why do these errors happen? There are several common causes:

Electrical interference — many electronic devices close together can disturb each other's signals.

Crosstalk — the signal in one wire leaks into a neighbouring wire and muddles it.

Electrical surges — a sudden jump in electrical power, often caused by lightning, can scramble data.

Broken or damaged cables — a faulty wire can corrupt the signal passing through it.
concepts.example: Here is a real example. Horizon Distributors' Hargeisa computer wants to send the byte 01000101. But one cable is faulty, so the receiving computer gets 00000101 instead. Look carefully at the second bit: it flipped from a 1 to a 0. That single change is an error. If nobody checked for it, the wrong data would be used. So how does a computer catch an error like this? That is what the next idea solves.

concepts.title: Echo Check: Catching Errors
concepts.explanation:
One method a computer can use to detect errors is called an echo check. An echo check is an error-detection method that compares two sets of data to see whether they match. Here are the steps:

The sender transmits the data to the receiver.

The receiver sends a copy of the data it received back to the sender (this returned copy is the 'echo').

The sender compares the returned copy with the original data it sent.

If the two match, the sender knows the data arrived without errors.

If the two are different, the sender knows an error occurred, and it can send the data again to try to correct it.

Here is an echo check in action, using a short piece of binary. In the first case the copy matches, so the data is good. In the second case one bit is different, so an error is found:

Echo check: compare the data sent with the copy returned

echo = 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 0 -> MATCH -> data is correct

echo = 1 0 0 1 0 1 0 1 -> DIFFERENT (bit 5) -> send again
concepts.example: An echo check is simple and useful, but it has a cost: the data must travel the network twice (there and back), which uses more time and bandwidth. It is also not perfect — if the returned copy is itself corrupted, the check can be fooled. Even so, it is a clear, easy way to spot most errors, and it shows the key idea behind all error checking: compare, and resend if something is wrong.

concepts.title: Encryption: Turning Messages into Secret Code
concepts.explanation:
Data travelling across a network can be intercepted — secretly captured — on the way. If a message is sent as ordinary plaintext, anyone who captures it can read it. Imagine the Hargeisa office sending "Customer PIN is 4471" as plaintext. A hacker who grabbed it would see the PIN at once. This is exactly what worries Maya about the messages travelling between Hargeisa and Mogadishu.

Encryption solves this. It scrambles the message into cipher text that looks like nonsense. The message can still be intercepted, but now the hacker cannot understand it. Only someone with the correct key can decrypt it back into readable plaintext. To agree how to scramble and unscramble, the two devices share an algorithm (a set of steps) and a key.

One famous, simple cipher is the Caesar cipher, named after Julius Caesar, who really used it over 2000 years ago to protect his military messages. It works by shifting each letter along the alphabet by a fixed number of places. In Year 8 we will use a shift of 3 to the right: A becomes D, B becomes E, C becomes F, and so on. When you reach the end, you wrap around, so X becomes A, Y becomes B, and Z becomes C. The key is simply the number 3.

Here is the full table. The top row is the plaintext letter; the bottom row is the cipher letter you write instead:

To encrypt, find each plaintext letter in the top row and write the letter below it. For example, the word HELLO encrypts to KHOOR (H becomes K, E becomes H, L becomes O, L becomes O, O becomes R). To decrypt, do the opposite: find the cipher letter and read the plaintext above it. As another example, the word FRIEND encrypts to IULHQG. You will practise encrypting and decrypting a full Hargeisa-to-Mogadishu message in your Activities booklet.

Real websites do not use the Caesar cipher — it is far too easy to crack, because there are only 25 possible shifts to try. Real encryption uses keys so large that even the fastest computers would take billions of years to break them. But the Caesar cipher shows the exact idea behind all encryption: turn readable text into a secret that only the right key can unlock.

The 's' in HTTPS and the little padlock in your browser's address bar mean the website is using strong encryption. Everything you type - passwords, messages, payment details - is scrambled before it leaves your device and only unscrambled when it safely arrives. That is why you should always look for the padlock before typing anything private.

concepts.title: Threats: Viruses, Spyware and Hackers
concepts.explanation:
Every time you download a file — an email attachment, an image, an app — there is a small risk it carries something harmful. To protect Horizon Distributors, you first need to know what the threats are.

A virus is software that can corrupt (damage) or delete data on a computer. It can hide inside almost any download: an image, a document, even a video.

Spyware is software that secretly records what someone does on their computer — for example, which keys they press on the keyboard. It then sends this information to a cybercriminal (someone who commits crime using the internet), who can study it to discover things like passwords and PINs.

A hacker is someone who tries to gain unauthorised access to a network or data — that is, access they are not allowed to have. A hacker might try to send harmful data to a computer to break into it and steal information.
concepts.example: The good news is that for every threat there is a defence. The next two sections cover the three tools that protect most computers: a firewall, antivirus software and antispyware software.

concepts.title: Firewalls: A Guard at the Door
concepts.explanation:
A firewall acts as a barrier for your computer or network — like a bodyguard standing at the door to your data. A firewall can be hardware-based (a physical device) or software-based (a program on your device); both do the same job.

The firewall has a set of rules about what data is allowed in and out. When data is sent to your computer, it arrives at the firewall first. The firewall checks whether the data meets the rules. If it does, the data is allowed through. If it does not — for example, if it looks like a hacker trying to break in — the firewall blocks it and stops it reaching your computer.

A firewall checks data against its rules before letting it in

+----------------+ meets the rules? +-------------+

| FIREWALL | ---------- YES --------> | computer |

| (checks rules)| ---------- NO ---------> | BLOCKED |

+----------------+ +-------------+
concepts.example: So a firewall is like a guard who checks everyone at the door and only lets in those who are allowed. For Horizon Distributors, a firewall is the first line of defence against hackers trying to reach the office network from the internet.

concepts.title: Antivirus and Antispyware: Scanning for Danger
concepts.explanation:
A firewall guards the door, but some harmful software may still slip in inside a file you chose to download. That is where antivirus and antispyware software come in. They are both types of software, and they work in the same way: they scan files to check for danger. Antivirus looks for viruses; antispyware looks for spyware.

There are two main times they scan:

When you download a file. The software scans the file before you open it. If it finds a virus, a warning message appears, and you can choose not to open or keep the file.

Regular scans of stored files. The software can check all the files already on the computer. If it finds a virus, it will either delete it or move it to a special area called quarantine — a bit like a prison for data. A virus in quarantine can no longer corrupt or delete anything, and you can review it and delete it safely later.

One golden rule: scan every file you download, even from people you trust. A virus can hide in any kind of file, and a friend may pass one on without realising. Most school and office computers scan automatically, but if you are unsure whether a computer does, check with a trusted adult. Keeping antivirus and antispyware switched on and up to date is one of the simplest, strongest things Horizon Distributors — and you — can do to stay safe.

"I will describe a security tool - a firewall, antivirus or antispyware - in my own words, and you tell me which one I mean and whether my description is correct. Then swap: you describe one and I will name it."

Teaching the idea back is the best test of whether you really understand it.

Staying Safe and Responsible Online

Understanding how networks and security work also means knowing how to behave safely and kindly online. Values like trustworthiness, honesty and respecting other people's privacy make you a safe and responsible person online. Here is how to put them into practice:

Guard your private information. Never share your full name, home address, school, phone number, passwords or PINs with people you do not know online.

Use strong, private passwords. A strong password is long and mixes letters, numbers and symbols. Use a different one for important accounts, and never share it — not even with a friend.

Check before you trust. Look for https and the padlock before typing anything private into a website, especially an online shop.

Scan what you download, and keep antivirus, antispyware and your firewall switched on. Do not ignore security warnings.

Be trustworthy with others' data. If someone shares something private with you, keep it private. Do not spread other people's information or photos without permission — that is a matter of trust and respect.

Think before you type. Be kind and honest in messages. Words online can be saved and shared, so write only what you would be happy for anyone to read.
concepts.example: Ask a trusted adult if anything online worries you, scares you, or does not feel right. You are never in trouble for asking.

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work

rules.title: ! - Three questions for any network
rules.text: For a PAN, a LAN or a WAN, ask three things: How many devices can it have? Where are the devices located? Who owns the network hardware? Answer those three and you can describe any network type.

rules.title: ! - Star is the office favourite
rules.text: Most office and school LANs use a star topology: every device plugs into a central switch. If one cable breaks, only that device is affected - but if the switch fails, the whole network goes down.

rules.title: ! - Copper carries electricity, fibre carries light
rules.text: Copper is cheap and easy but slower and can suffer interference. Fibre is fast, immune to interference and great for long distances, but more expensive.

rules.title: ! - Echo check: compare and resend
rules.text: An echo check sends a copy of the data back and compares it. Same means no error; different means an error, so the data is sent again. It detects errors - it does not fix them by itself.

rules.title: ! - Three guards for your data
rules.text: A firewall blocks unsafe data at the door. Antivirus finds and removes viruses. Antispyware finds and removes spyware. Encryption keeps the data secret even if it is intercepted. Use them together.

terms: network
A group of devices connected together so they can share data.
network hardware
The physical parts needed to build a network, such as cables and routers.
PAN
Personal area network - a tiny network around one person's own devices.
LAN
Local area network - devices connected within one building or site.
WAN
Wide area network - devices connected across a large area, even worldwide.
ISP
Internet service provider - a company that provides an internet connection.
topology
The shape or layout in which the devices in a network are connected.
switch
A device that connects devices in a LAN and directs data to the right one.
router
A device that connects a network to other networks, such as the internet.
copper cable
A cable of copper wire that carries data as electrical signals.
fibre optic cable
A cable of thin glass that carries data as pulses of light.
interference
Anything that disturbs a signal, such as walls or other electrical signals.
crosstalk
When the signal in one wire leaks into and disturbs a nearby wire.
bandwidth
The amount of data that can be sent in a certain amount of time.
data packet
A small labelled chunk that data is broken into to travel across a network.
protocol
An agreed set of rules for how devices send data to each other.
error
A mistake in data, often a bit flipping from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0, during transfer.
echo check
An error-detection method that compares sent data with a returned copy.
encryption
Scrambling data with a key so only the right person can read it.
plaintext
A message before it is encrypted - one that can be read easily.
cipher text
A message after it has been encrypted - scrambled and unreadable.
Caesar cipher
A simple cipher that shifts each letter along the alphabet by a fixed amount.
firewall
Hardware or software that checks data and blocks anything unsafe.
virus
Software that can corrupt (damage) or delete data on a computer.

Network Topologies: The Shape of a Network Once you have several devices in a LAN, you must decide how to arrange the connections between them. The layout, or shape, of a network is called its topology. Choosing a topology is a real decision when you design a network, so Horizon Distributors will need to pick one for its office.
